new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable that begins with a consonant: consonant-initial words are stressed on the first syllable (máta, kérindja), vowel-initial words (the initial-dropped ones) on the second syllable (abó, arábin). This is onset-conditioned rather than count-based, so on the catalog's own standard (Mbabaram, Alyawarr, Lamu-Lamu) it is coded weight-sensitive; the positional restatement would be 'initial unless the word begins with a vowel, then peninitial'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Agwamin. Goedemans' own view (ch. 5) is that this pattern is a historical artefact of initial dropping (a prior shift of stress to the second syllable followed by loss of the initial CV), i.e. the onset-conditioning is diachronic in origin.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (isolated lexical items, four accent-marked words). The Agwamin forms carry no source ('No reference' in App. D); they are presented as an instance of the Mbabaram/Aranda type in which stress is on the first syllable that has an onset (first postconsonantal syllable).
new_statements.identity_note: The only stress data found are labelled 'Agwamin' (Goedemans 1998; AIATSIS Y132), whereas the catalog key wami1239/ISO wmi is 'Wamin' (AIATSIS Y133). Sutton 1976 treats them as one language ('Hereafter I refer to Wamin/Agwamin as Wamin'; per Fred Fulford 'two mutually intelligible dialects, one heavy and one light'), and Glottolog wami1239 lists Agwamin as an alternate name, so the Agwamin statement applies to wami1239 as a whole; no separate glottocode exists for Agwamin.

new_statements.quote: The languages of north-east Queensland can be roughly divided into two (non-genetic) groupings: 1. a phonologically intact group whose words mostly or always begin with consonants, which mostly have three phonemic vowels, no fricatives, no complex syllable onsets, no word-final stops, word-stress on the first syllable and a common minimal word-structure CVCV; and 2. an aberrant group whose words may begin with vowels, which mostly have five or more phonemic vowels, which may have fricatives, complex syllable onsets, word-final stops, word-stress on non-initial syllables, and which have common word-structures VC, VCV, CV, CCVC etc.

Einaslei…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog: the catalog rule (stress on the first syllable that begins with a consonant, Goedemans 1998 ex. 26 abó, arábin) puts stress on a non-initial syllable in the vowel-initial words that initial dropping produces, which is exactly the group property Sutton states. But it is a characterisation of the aberrant group as a whole, not a Wamin-specific rule, and it does not state the onset condition, so it adds no independent Wamin evidence; language-specific reading stays none found.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No Wamin- or Agwamin-specific stress statement anywhere in chapter 2 (printed pp. 24-67, the only part about Wamin/Agwamin). The thesis's only stress statement bearing on the language is group-level: the 'aberrant' (initial-dropping) languages of north-east Queensland, among which Sutton explicitly places Agwamin-Wamin, have 'word-stress on non-initial syllables', versus first-syllable stress in 'intact' languages. The 'Word stress' section 3.2 and the sentence 'Primary stress falls on the first syllable' (p. 67, sec. 2.8) describe Gugu-Badhun, not Wamin. Sutton's data base for Agwamin was 'less than twenty words' (p. 66) and 'Wamin has never been recorded (the informant gave only one word /ndjil/ "food"..)' (p. 67).
new_statements.exceptions: none for Wamin; the group statement is hedged ('roughly divided', 'may begin with vowels').
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog wami1239 covers both Agwamin and Wamin. Sutton 1973 pp. 66-67 treats them as 'mutually intelligible dialects, though distinct' on the word of a Palm Island Wamin speaker (1970), notes that Tindale's 'Wagaman' wordlist is 85% identical to his Agwamin list and probably Wamin (fn. 11, p. 72: Tindale's informant Charlie Oak Park was probably a Wamin), and that Dixon's 'Wagaman' (whose informants called their language 'Agwamin') is an intact Gugu-Yalandji-type language, not Agwamin. The group-level stress statement applies to Sutton's 'aberrant' Einasleigh Pama Group (Mbabaram, Agwamin, Wamin), i.e. to the whole wami1239 languoid.
